item.title: Public Health reminds families Summer EBT benefits expire Nov. 16
item.description: The Department of Public Health and Social Services is reminding families who received 2026 Summer Electronic Benefit Transfer benefits to use any remaining funds by Nov. 16. The federally funded program helps eligible families purchase food for school-aged children during the summer months. Under federal requirements, any unused benefits will be returned to the funding source after the expiration
item.content:encoded:
The Department of Public Health and Social Services is reminding families who received 2026 Summer Electronic Benefit Transfer benefits to use any remaining funds by Nov. 16.

The federally funded program helps eligible families purchase food for school-aged children during the summer months. Under federal requirements, any unused benefits will be returned to the funding source after the expiration date.

Families are encouraged to check their card balances and use their remaining benefits before Nov. 16. However, those who received their child’s card later and were given a different expiration date should follow the date provided.

Families who have not picked up their child’s Summer EBT card or need a replacement may visit the Bureau of Economic Security office on the second floor of the RanCare Building in Tamuning from 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.Monday through Friday.

For assistance, families may contact the Summer EBT Call Center at (671)735-7325 or (671)735-7310, or email kidssebtguam@dphss.guam.gov .

Public Health administers the Summer EBT Program locally in partnership with the Guam Department of Education.

item.title: Hybrid Land Use Commission approves school in Tumon, extension for Tamuning subdivision
item.description: The Guam Hybrid Land Use Commission on Thursday approved using a vacant mall in Tumon as a school and granted a one-year extension for the construction of a subdivision in Tamuning. The zone variance allows the unused Tumon Bay Mall, owned by Grandview Development, to be converted to a facility that will house 40 classrooms and up to 1,080 students from iLearn Academy, a charter school.
item.content:encoded:
The Guam Hybrid Land Use Commission on Thursday approved using a vacant mall in Tumon as a school and granted a one-year extension for the construction of a subdivision in Tamuning.

The zone variance allows the unused Tumon Bay Mall, owned by Grandview Development, to be converted to a facility that will house 40 classrooms and up to 1,080 students from iLearn Academy, a charter school.

Architect Michael Blas Makio, managing principal at Taniguchi Ruth Makio Architects, said the project would be good for Tumon and good for education.

“Even driving here, we started the really sad exercise of counting the vacant buildings that we're seeing around the island, and that's a really scary growing number, right? So we’ve got to find these viable uses that we can bring into the space,” Makio said.

The vacant mall is located next to Garden Villa Hotel and across from Crowne Plaza Resort.

The Commission also granted a one-year extension for the construction of Oka Villas subdivision, located near Oka Pay-Less and Rosie’s Apartments in Tamuning.

The land has been cleared and utilities are being installed.

The subdivision will have 36 single-family residential lots, a playground and a percolation basin.

item.title: Medicaid program serves more than half of CNMI population, annual report shows
item.description: The Commonwealth Medicaid Agency reported significant gains in healthcare coverage, federal funding and operational modernization during fiscal year 2026, highlighting its role as one of the CNMI's largest healthcare safety-net programs. According to the CMA’s report, the agency served 23,690 active Medicaid beneficiaries during the reporting period, representing about 50% of the CNMI's population
item.content:encoded:
The Commonwealth Medicaid Agency reported significant gains in healthcare coverage, federal funding and operational modernization during fiscal year 2026, highlighting its role as one of the CNMI's largest healthcare safety-net programs.

According to the CMA’s report, the agency served 23,690 active Medicaid beneficiaries during the reporting period, representing about 50% of the CNMI's population based on the 2020 U.S. Census and nearly 54% of the territory's estimated 2026 population.

The report said enrollment included individuals who maintained coverage through continuity-of-coverage provisions tied to public health emergency declarations following Super Typhoons Sinlaku and Bavi. The agency described Medicaid as a critical healthcare safety net that supports more than half of the Commonwealth's residents.

Among the year's major accomplishments was the approval of four disaster-relief state plan amendments by the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services. The amendments support disaster-related healthcare coverage, behavioral health services and provider reimbursement. The agency also reported that federal legislation authorized an additional $21.4 million for FY 2026 Medicaid expenditures.

The report highlighted several modernization efforts, including CMS approval of the agency's FY 2026 Advance Planning Document and continued development of Medicaid information technology systems. CMA also established electronic provider enrollment portals, digitized workflow processes and upgraded office internet infrastructure from DSL to fiber service. Agency officials reported no network outages following relocation to a new facility.

Provider participation also expanded during the fiscal year. The agency approved 57 provider enrollment applications from the CNMI, Guam and the U.S. mainland, while continuing the use of letters of agreement to facilitate off-island specialty care unavailable locally. CMA processed 203 of 213 requests involving such agreements.

In its financial report, the agency reported a FY 2026 approved budget of nearly $67 million for Medical Assistance Payments and total reimbursement costs of approximately $89.7 million. On-island reimbursement expenditures totaled about $72.3 million, while off-island reimbursements amounted to roughly $17.4 million.

The agency also emphasized workforce development, reporting 18 new hires, three workforce program conversions to permanent agency positions and continued employee training initiatives. Total staffing increased from 40 to 41 employees.

Looking ahead, CMA said its priorities include implementing a new eligibility and enrollment system, expanding healthcare access through a proposed state plan amendment addressing coverage for foreign healthcare providers, pursuing a potential Section 1115 Medicaid demonstration waiver and strengthening provider compliance oversight. The agency also plans to continue exploring additional federal funding opportunities and improvements to behavioral health services.

Agency Director George J. Cruz said the agency remained focused on accountability, transparency and operational improvements while ensuring continued access to healthcare services for eligible residents throughout the Commonwealth.

item.title: 'Punch in the gut': Homes sales fall to their lowest in 16 years
item.description: The housing market has finally broken out of the stagnant holding pattern it's been stuck in for more than four years – just not in the right direction. Existing home sales in October fell to 3.75 million, making an 8.8% decline in sales from a year earlier, according to the National Association of Realtors. The last time sales were this low was 16 years ago.
item.content:encoded:
The housing market has finally broken out of the stagnant holding pattern it's been stuck in for more than four years – just not in the right direction.

Existing home sales in October fell to 3.75 million, making an 8.8% decline in sales from a year earlier, according to the National Association of Realtors. The last time sales were this low was 16 years ago.

"It was a punch in the gut," said Joel Berner, senior economist at Realtor.com . "We expected to see a soft month but not the softest month since 2010."

The drop is mainly due to high mortgage rates.

In October, the average rate for a 30-year fixed rate mortgage hit as high as 7.40%, the highest since 2023. Rates have gone down a bit since then, but are still well above where they were a year ago.

Higher inflation and bond yields have driven up mortgage rates, but some of this housing slowdown was by design.

The Federal Reserve raised its benchmark interest rate in September to increase the cost of borrowing, including home mortgages. Fewer home sales and other purchases mean less economic activity, which the Fed wants in order to reach its goal of lowering inflation.

Policymakers at the Fed have signaled another rate hike could come in December, which could further slow down the housing market.

"It might seem like kicking the housing market while it's down right now for the Fed to continue a rate raising cycle but in the long run getting inflation under control is really the goal," Berner said.

item.title: Casualties continue to rise after Brooklyn building collapses
item.description: The New York City Fire Department reported Thursday that more victims had been found after a three-story residential building in the Flatbush neighborhood of Brooklyn collapsed a day earlier. Mayor Zohran Mamdani said six people had been declared dead at the scene. Two others died in a hospital. 18 other people were injured in the building collapse.
item.content:encoded:
The New York City Fire Department reported Thursday that more victims had been found after a three-story residential building in the Flatbush neighborhood of Brooklyn collapsed a day earlier.

Mayor Zohran Mamdani said six people had been declared dead at the scene. Two others died in a hospital. 18 other people were injured in the building collapse.

Search efforts are continuing with more than 250 firefighters and emergency workers deployed to the site, according to city officials.

item.title: BTS is boycotting the Grammys. It's part of a long history of category controversies
item.description: Almost every single year, the Recording Academy updates the terminology and categories that it uses to recognize musicians at its annual Grammy Awards. In 2026, five new categories were introduced — including an award that sparked backlash from one of the most popular groups in the world: BTS . The best Asian pop music performance category, which will debut its inaugural slate of nominees next wee
item.content:encoded:
Almost every single year, the Recording Academy updates the terminology and categories that it uses to recognize musicians at its annual Grammy Awards. In 2026, five new categories were introduced — including an award that sparked backlash from one of the most popular groups in the world: BTS .

The best Asian pop music performance category, which will debut its inaugural slate of nominees next week, was created to award "contemporary popular music originating from or widely recognized within Asian markets, including K-Pop, J-Pop, and C-Pop." But just over a month after the Recording Academy unveiled its plans for the award, which requires "meaningful use of one or more Asian languages" for eligibility, the K-pop boyband BTS shared its own announcement on social media.

"We have decided not to submit for Grammys this year. Rather than music being divided by region or language, we hope music itself can be heard and loved for what it is," the band wrote. "We are always grateful to [our fandom] ARMY and everyone who is always with us."

The band is in the middle of a massive comeback following a years-long hiatus for its members' mandatory military service in South Korea. They released the album Arirang in March and embarked on a sold-out global tour soon after. Following BTS' statement, the K-pop group Stray Kids also announced its intent to not submit.

Recording Academy CEO Harvey Mason Jr. responded to BTS' statement on Instagram, writing that he was saddened but respected the group's decision.

"I do want to clarify something that seems to be getting lost in the conversation," Mason Jr. wrote . "The Asian Pop category was created to celebrate the depth, diversity and extraordinary growth of pop artistry coming out of Asia. The spirit of this new category is to shine a dedicated spotlight on these important artists. More categories mean more artists' work is recognized. It's never to divide, but to expand who is recognized by our 15,000 Grammy voters."

The back-and-forth between BTS and the Recording Academy marks the latest thread in a longer, complicated lineage of the Grammys' attempts to become more inclusive.

BTS has been nominated for five Grammys in the past, including several nods for best pop duo/group performance, but has never won. Mathieu Berbiguier, a visiting assistant professor of Korean studies at Carnegie Mellon University, says the new category is a double-edged sword: on one hand, it's an opportunity to highlight music from across the Asian continent, which is growing in popularity as streaming and social media collapse borders in global listening habits. At the same time, Bebiguier says the category seems like an attempt to sideline the gains made by K-pop in recent years away from the general categories. (This past February, the viral hit "Golden" from the film KPop Demon Hunters became the first K-pop song to win a Grammy).

"Given that the term K-pop in itself hasn't been created in Korea, it's a category that has been created in difference, in comparison to other genres," Berbiguier says. "It is difficult to think of it as something positive, because it's kind of saying we want to acknowledge you, but at the same time in a separate category, so that it doesn't mix up with what is supposed to be mainstream."

Berbiguier points to the contention behind K-pop as a label, a catch-all signifier used by the foreign entertainment industry in an attempt to define popular music within South Korea that's also applied to acts from other countries (see, the "global girl group" Katseye ). Berbiguier himself defines K-pop not as a genre, but as a system in which young people are recruited into the Korean pop industry, given extensive training to sing, act or dance and later officially debuted either as a solo act or as part of a group.

What is considered K-pop is slippery, he explains, and even those within the system are considering shedding the label. Bang Si-Hyuk, founder of the South Korean conglomerate HYBE (which is behind several blockbuster K-pop groups, including BTS), said in a 2023 interview with Maeil Business Newspaper that the "K" might need to be dropped in order to continue expanding the genre's global appeal. RM, one of the members of BTS, told Rolling Stone that it's "an important debate" for the music industry.

"It shows you that the agenda is not the same on the side of the K-pop entertainment companies and the Grammys, because the Grammys probably think of it as a gateway to get more international recognition," Berbiguier says. "But then for the K-pop entertainment companies, that's not what they want. They want to be recognized as a whole."

The questions raised by the introduction of the Asian pop music category — what does it mean to separate music by location, race or language? Who gets to define that region's musical identity? And does the attempt to be inclusive ultimately cement an act's outsider status? — have all been raised before at different points in the Grammys' history.

Since the Awards' inception in 1959, the Recording Academy has faced criticism for how it racializes and represents popular music in the United States and abroad. Only 12 Black artists have ever won the most prestigious award of album of the year, and Black musicians have long called out the Academy for pigeonholing them into smaller categories that they say minimize their contributions. The Academy did not acknowledge the rise of hip-hop until 1988, when it first introduced the best rap performance category, but was soon met with controversy when it chose not to televise the award during the 1989 ceremony. As a result, artists including LL Cool J, Public Enemy and DJ Jazzy Jeff & The Fresh Prince — who ended up winning the Grammy — boycotted the ceremony in protest.

In 2016, Frank Ocean declined to submit his chart-topping album, Blonde , for consideration, calling the awards' nomination and voting system "dated" and calling it his "Colin Kaepernick" moment. The pop auteur had already been nominated seven times in several categories by that point and had won twice, including for best urban contemporary album in 2013. In 2020, Tyler, the Creator took home his first golden gramophone for best rap album for IGOR . During a press conference backstage, he said he was grateful for the award but felt that the category he was placed in was a sort of "backhanded compliment."

"It sucks that whenever we — and I mean guys that look like me — do anything that's genre-bending or that's anything they always put it in a rap or urban category. I don't like that 'urban' word — it's just a politically correct way to say the N-word to me," Tyler said.

Six months later, the Academy announced it would be dropping the "urban" term and renaming it to best progressive R&B album in an attempt to be more accurate and inclusive. John Vilanova, music scholar and journalism professor at Lehigh University, says there's always been an underlying tension between the narrative the Grammys want to tell about the music industry and the reality of what's happening in the culture.

"They're not at the bleeding edge and they're kind of not designed to be. It's a legacy product," he says. "So when they're making these adjustments, it is often in this kind of stumbling, bumbling way."

When it comes to smaller genres outside the mainstream, other issues arise. In 2011, the Recording Academy announced an overhaul that would cut back from 109 to 78 categories, doing away with male versus female awards in favor of gender-neutral categories and consolidating the number of awards in certain genres. Categories for Native American music, as well as Zydeco and Cajun music, were all merged into best regional roots music. Latin jazz was rolled into best jazz album. Regional Mexican categories were also impacted. In protest, four Latin jazz musicians — Bobby Sanabria, Mark Levine, Ben Lapidus and Eugene Marlow — filed a class-action lawsuit against the Recording Academy, claiming that the changes took away potential recognition and impacted their ability to make a living. The lawsuit was later dismissed by a New York judge, but the category was reinstated .

During the 2011 changes, the category then known as "world music" (now global) was also cut in half, down from two awards (contemporary versus traditional) to a single one. Ian Brennan produced the album that won in the consolidated best world music album category in 2012, Tassil by Tinariwen. But he says the collapse of the global category slashed global representation at the Grammys in half, and pushed out many smaller, regional musicians who could no longer compete against bigger names.

"It's a very complicated category because it includes the whole globe," Brennan says. "There's no category that has greater diversity or should have greater diversity than this category. But what we see is so much redundancy."

He says the same artists and countries often end up being represented in the global categories — Angelique Kidjo has received 10 nominations, Anoushka Shankar has been nominated nine times, and hugely influential genres, such as Ethiopian jazz, have never been recognized.

In recent years, the Academy has widened the global field to include several more awards: best global music album, best global music performance and in 2024, best African music performance . The new Asian pop category is supposed to further expand this inclusion.

Vilanova says that despite its less-than-smooth track record, the Recording Academy has taken serious steps to diversify its voting body and, in turn, the music it represents. Earlier this year, Bad Bunny made history when DeBÍ TiRAR MáS FOToS , his genre-bending homage to the history and sounds of Puerto Rico, became the first Spanish-language album to win album of the year.

The Chinese singer Miist, who is a voting member of the Recording Academy, says she understands the criticisms lobbed at the new Asian pop category — but as a smaller artist who records in multiple languages, including Mandarin, English and Spanish, she says she feels excited about submitting to the new category.

"It gives us an opportunity to showcase our music, which almost could have never had a chance to be heard by maybe 15,000 or 16,000 voting members," she says. "They would have never had a chance to be discovered. It also gives the voting members a chance to experience these different cultures and music."

She says the Academy could've done a better job of communicating about the changes and actively including more Asian musicians in the process. But as an artist and member who has now been internally involved in discussions about the global categories as a whole, she feels this is a step in the right direction.

"The Academy has to stand at a place that represents what the members want, what the musicians want. [It's] not necessarily the same thing as what the market wants. So I can see that the Academy is trying hard to balance the two, but I think we need to give them some time to get there."

item.title: Democrats want to stop Trump's arch, golf course and more. What are their options?
item.description: President Trump's efforts to remake Washington, D.C., have dominated his second term, even after his party's resounding midterm defeat. He started his election week at the scandal-plagued Reflecting Pool and ended it with an order declaring his gilded Oval Office a national monument to "make it impossible for anybody ever to destroy this incredible space."
item.content:encoded:
President Trump's efforts to remake Washington, D.C., have dominated his second term, even after his party's resounding midterm defeat.

He started his election week at the scandal-plagued Reflecting Pool and ended it with an order declaring his gilded Oval Office a national monument to "make it impossible for anybody ever to destroy this incredible space."

That proclamation, like any executive order, could be undone by a future president. But many of Trump's construction projects are changing D.C. in more permanent ways.

His administration has already downed hundreds of trees at East Potomac Park and demolished the East Wing of the White House to make space for a ballroom — which he called "the safest place in Washington" as he showed it to reporters the day after the midterms.

Trump has taken a uniquely unilateral approach to construction , packing regulatory commissions with his allies and bypassing Congress entirely. Most of his projects — from the triumphal arch to the Kennedy Center — are now playing out in court .

Critics accuse the Trump administration of skirting federal laws and misleading judges in its effort to progress as quickly as possible before the end of his term.

Democrats have vowed to use their soon-to-be congressional majority to push back on what they describe as Trump's "vanity projects."

When asked about that, White House spokesperson Davis Ingle told NPR in an email that "no other president has done more to beautify our Nation's interior than President Trump." He cited park cleanups, the Reflecting Pool and the White House helipad and ballroom as examples, and said Democrats "should work with President Trump to make our nation's capital beautiful again."

Rep. Jared Huffman, D.-Calif., told NPR in an interview that the Trump administration has "played this game of Catch Me If You Can, where they roll ahead with the bulldozers and the tree cutters … and they wait for courts to shut them down." He says a Democrat-led Congress will fight back.

"There's no way that we could look away while these sacred, iconic places are being permanently changed in ways that violate the law and could have really terrible lasting impacts," said Huffman, the top Democrat on the House Natural Resources Committee, which has a legislative purview over public lands and national parks.

Huffman says blocking Trump's construction projects — and holding people accountable for potential wrongdoing — will be a top priority when he leads the committee. Earlier this week, he sent letters ordering dozens of administration officials and private companies to preserve their records for a future investigation.

"Whether it is the arch or … or the East Potomac golf course or any number of other examples around the United States capital, that is federal land, and we have a direct statutory responsibility to either authorize those changes or to stop them if they're proceeding without the proper authorization," Huffman said.

What would that actually look like? Democrats have many tools at their disposal, from legislation to lawsuits. But experts say only two are likely to succeed: funding and oversight.

Congress could — at least in theory — pass laws to block specific projects from moving ahead. Some Democratic lawmakers have already introduced bills to protect the Kennedy Center from demolition and prohibit the construction of an arch at Memorial Circle.

But Trump has promised to " veto everything ," and Democrats won't have a big enough majority to override him on their own.

"Legislation in principle is the cleanest way of doing it, but it's also not achievable," said David Super, who teaches administrative and constitutional law at Georgetown. "So what they're likely to do is cut off funds."

The Constitution says that the federal government may spend money only if is appropriated by Congress. But Trump has neither sought nor received congressional authorization for projects like the arch and the White House ballroom — he maintains he doesn't need it.

Rep. Chellie Pingree of Maine is one of many who disagree. She's the top Democrat on the House committee that oversees funding for the Interior Department.

"Certainly Congress should have been involved, because we have the power of the purse," Pingree told NPR. "That is our ultimate tool. And Republicans have refused to use that. But we can use that in very many ways to block him or to use it for leverage."

Pingree says a Democratic majority will be able to write appropriations bills with clear language from the outset about where money can and can't be spent — and potentially take the president to court if he doesn't follow it.

Super expects Congress would prevail in such a challenge, because it has clear-cut authority over federal funds.

For example, he noted that some of Trump's D.C.-area beautification projects have been funded at least in part by diverted national park entrance fees . Congress could "cap how much money can be used in the greater Washington area, and force the money to be used in the Everglades and Yosemite and Great Smoky Mountains," he said.

Congress will have to make some appropriations decisions in the coming weeks, since it needs to pass a short-term funding bill by Dec. 11 to avoid a government shutdown. Democrats could use that opportunity to try to limit funding for at least one of Trump's construction projects.

Huffman has proposed language that would prevent Trump from using federal funds for the East Potomac golf course renovations, limiting them instead to repairs of the park's crumbling seawall. Pingree said she will join him in fighting to negotiate that into next month's bill.

"Whether or not the president will sign that with that in there, I don't know yet," she said. "But certainly those are the most … immediate crisis points … People want the president to stop cutting down the trees on the golf course and stop trying to take that over, and they want to make sure that no shovel goes into the ground on building the arch."

Earlier this year Pingree introduced an amendment that would have outright blocked construction of the arch; it failed along party lines. She wonders whether any Republicans might vote differently after the midterms, given the message Americans sent at the polls.

"They want the president to be focused on the issues they're dealing with: the cost of health care, the cost of food, the cost of gasoline," she said. "And if every time the president gives a speech, he's either standing in front of the Reflecting Pool, which he spent millions of dollars on, or showing you the new marble choices he's putting into the ballroom, it just makes a lot of people mad."

Pingree said she's been surprised to hear how strongly people feel about these projects – even people well outside D.C. And she agrees with them that potential corruption and misuse of taxpayer dollars are worth fighting: "After the first of the year, we will use every tool in our toolbox."

Lawmakers and experts acknowledge that not every project is reversible, or potentially even worth the fight. Huffman suggested he will focus on bigger projects, and ones that are moving too fast for courts to adequately rein in.

"Are we going to throw all of our efforts at stopping the gilding of every statue in Washington, D.C.? Probably not," said Huffman. "But these are iconic places that we're talking about, with permanent damage that we need to engage on to try to prevent."
